questions.question: How does useState work and when should you use a functional update?
questions.title: useState and functional updates
questions.direct_answer: `useState` gives a component memory between renders. It returns the current render's state snapshot and a setter that queues the next state. Pass a value when replacing state independently, and pass an updater such as `setCount(count => count + 1)` when the next value depends on pending previous state.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner understands render snapshots, queued updates, and immutable state changes.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Expecting a state variable to change immediately in the running handler or deriving dependent updates from a stale snapshot.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Trace direct and functional updates through the same queue.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `useState(initialValue)` returns the current state and a setter.
The setter queues another render; it does not rewrite the current snapshot.
Use an updater when the next value depends on previous state.
Queued updater functions are applied in order.
Replace objects and arrays instead of mutating existing state.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`useState` adds local memory to a function component. Calling `const [count, setCount] = useState(0)` gives the current render a `count` snapshot and gives the component a setter that can request a future value. The initial argument is used for the first render of that component position.

Calling the setter queues an update and another render; it does not change the variable inside the event handler already running. That handler closes over one render's snapshot, so logging `count` immediately after `setCount` still shows the earlier value even though the next render will receive the queued result.

If the next state does not depend on previous state, a direct replacement such as `setOpen(true)` is clear. If it does depend on previous state, I use an updater function such as `setCount(current => current + 1)`. React queues that function and later gives it the pending state.

For example, starting from zero, two calls to `setCount(count + 1)` both calculate one from the same snapshot. Two calls to `setCount(current => current + 1)` are processed in order: zero becomes one, then one becomes two. This is about the source of the next value, not merely a syntax preference.

For an object or array, the next state must be a replacement value. `setUser(current => ({ ...current, name }))` creates a new object while preserving unchanged fields. Mutating the existing object damages earlier snapshots and can leave React with the same reference. So my rule is direct value for an independent replacement, updater function for a calculation from pending state, and immutable copies for compound values. If several transitions become difficult to describe, a reducer may express them more clearly.

sections.title: State is a snapshot, not a live variable
sections.content: Each render receives one fixed state value. Its handlers keep that value even after they queue updates. React processes the queue to produce the state snapshot for a later render.

sections.title: How the update queue changes the result
sections.content:
A direct setter argument is a request to replace the pending value. Repeating `setCount(count + 1)` therefore repeats the same replacement when both expressions read one snapshot. An updater is a calculation; each updater consumes the result produced by the previous queue entry.

React may batch updates from one interaction before rendering so the UI does not show half-finished state. Batching does not make the current variable mutable. It makes the queue model—and the distinction between a replacement and an updater—important.

sections.title: Two queued updater functions
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Current snapshot: 0] --> B[queue n => n + 1]
  B --> C[pending value: 1]
  C --> D[queue n => n + 1]
  D --> E[next render: 2]
```

sections.title: Increment twice from pending state
Boundary to remember
sections.content: An updater must be pure. React may call updater functions more than once in development to reveal accidental side effects. Calculate and return the next state; do not send requests, mutate external data, or modify the previous object inside it.

questions.question: Which values should be stored in React state?
questions.title: Choosing minimal React state
questions.direct_answer: Store a value in state when the component must remember it between renders and changing it should update the UI. Do not store constants, values available from props, or values that can be calculated from existing props and state. Keep one source of truth and choose a state shape that avoids impossible combinations.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can design state instead of putting every variable into useState.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Synchronizing a derived value with an Effect and creating stale or contradictory copies.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Reduce a concrete form or list to its smallest source-of-truth state.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: State remembers information that can change between renders.
A state change should matter to rendered output or interaction.
Calculate derived values during render instead of storing copies.
Avoid redundant and contradictory state variables.
Place each state value in the nearest component that owns it.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A value belongs in React state when the component needs to remember it between renders and a change should influence the rendered interface or future interaction. Examples include the text typed into a controlled input, the selected tab, or the identifier of an expanded panel.

I avoid state for values that never change, temporary variables used only during one calculation, and information already available from props or other state. If `firstName` and `lastName` are state, `fullName` is normally a calculation during render, not a third state variable that needs synchronization.

For example, a searchable product list may store `query` and `showInStockOnly`. The visible products can be calculated with `products.filter(...)` from those values and the products prop. Storing `filteredProducts` as state creates another copy that can become stale whenever products or either filter changes.

The state shape should also prevent contradictions. Instead of booleans such as `isLoading`, `hasError`, and `isSuccess` that can accidentally all be true, one status value such as `'idle'`, `'loading'`, `'success'`, or `'error'` describes mutually exclusive phases. Related values can be grouped when they always change together, but unrelated inputs need not share one object.

Ownership matters. Local hover or input state can stay near one component. A value used to coordinate siblings should move to their closest common parent and come back down as props. That creates one source of truth without making all application state global. My test is to remove the candidate state mentally. If it can be recalculated accurately from current inputs, it is derived. If forgetting it between renders would break the interaction, it is real state. The smallest complete state model is usually the easiest to keep correct.

sections.title: Store the source, calculate the view
sections.content: Minimal state contains the changing facts that cannot be recovered from current inputs. Everything else becomes a calculation, which removes synchronization code and prevents stale copies.

sections.title: Redundant state creates extra update paths
sections.content:
Every stored value needs a rule for keeping it current. If visible products are stored separately from products and filters, every update path must remember to rebuild them. Missing one path creates a bug even though all source values are correct.

A render calculation always uses one consistent snapshot of props and state. Derived data calculated there cannot lag behind that snapshot. If the calculation is genuinely expensive, measure it and consider memoizing it; an Effect plus state is still the wrong synchronization mechanism.

sections.title: One source produces the visible list
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[products prop] --> D[filter during render]
  B[query state] --> D
  C[in-stock state] --> D
  D --> E[visible products]
```

sections.title: Derive filtered products during render
Boundary to remember
sections.content: Do not reject all cached values as state. Data loaded from an external source, an unsaved user draft, or a snapshot intentionally kept for comparison can be legitimate state. The deciding question is whether it is an independent fact or merely another expression of current inputs.

questions.question: How do you update objects and arrays in React state?
questions.title: Immutable object and array state updates
questions.direct_answer: Treat objects and arrays in React state as read-only snapshots. Create a new object or array containing the required change, then pass that replacement to the setter. Use object spread for shallow field changes and array methods such as `map`, `filter`, and spread for items. Copy every nested level that actually changes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner understands snapshots, reference identity, and practical immutable updates.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Changing a nested property and spreading only the outer object after the old nested object was already mutated.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show add, update, and remove operations while preserving unrelated references.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Never mutate an object or array already stored in state.
Object spread makes a shallow replacement object.
Use `map` to replace items and `filter` to remove them.
Copy each changed level in a nested structure.
Keep state flatter when deep immutable updates become difficult.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Objects and arrays held in React state should be treated as read-only snapshots. JavaScript allows mutation, but changing the existing value does not express a new state transition to React and also changes data that an earlier render still conceptually owns. I create a replacement value and pass that to the setter.

For objects, a shallow field update can use spread: `setUser(user => ({ ...user, name: nextName }))`. The new outer object carries unchanged fields forward and replaces `name`. Spread is shallow, so changing `user.address.city` also requires a new address object rather than mutating the old nested address.

For arrays, I use non-mutating operations. Spread can append an item, `filter` can remove one, and `map` can replace a matching item while returning the unchanged items as they are. Methods such as `push`, `pop`, `splice`, `sort`, and `reverse` mutate their receiver, so they should operate on a copy if they are needed.

For example, to toggle one todo, I map the current array. The matching todo becomes `{ ...todo, done: !todo.done }`; every other item is returned unchanged. The setter receives a new array, the modified item has a new object, and unrelated items keep their identities.

The boundary is structure depth. Repeated nested spreads are easy to get wrong and often signal that state is too deeply nested or duplicates entities. Normalizing records by ID, splitting independent state, or using a reducer can make ownership and transitions clearer. A library such as Immer can provide mutation-like syntax while producing immutable results, but the underlying rule stays the same. The goal is not immutability as ceremony. Replacement values preserve reliable render snapshots, make changes explicit, and allow React and memoized components to use reference equality as a meaningful signal.

sections.title: A change creates a new path
sections.content: Only the object or array path that changes needs new references. Unchanged branches can be reused. This creates a next snapshot without rewriting the data seen by previous renders.

sections.title: Why a shallow copy is sometimes insufficient
sections.content:
`const next = { ...user }` copies only the outer object's properties. If `next.address` still refers to `user.address`, assigning `next.address.city` mutates the shared nested object. The correct update replaces `address` too.

State normalization reduces that work. Instead of deeply nesting each task inside a project inside a user, keep records keyed by ID and store relationships as IDs. Updating one record then replaces a short path rather than rebuilding a large nested tree.

sections.title: References after a nested update
sections.content:
Old user ──► old address ──► Pune
New user ──► new address ──► Jaipur
          └► same unchanged preferences object

sections.title: Add, update, and remove without mutation
Boundary to remember
sections.content: A local variable created during the current render can be mutated before it is exposed because no earlier snapshot owns it. The restriction concerns props, state, context, and other pre-existing values used as render inputs—not every use of mutation in JavaScript.

questions.question: When should you use useReducer instead of useState?
questions.title: useState versus useReducer
questions.direct_answer: Use `useState` for a few independent values with simple updates. Use `useReducer` when one state has several related transitions, the next result depends on multiple fields, or transition rules deserve one testable function. A reducer centralizes update logic; it does not automatically make state global, faster, or more correct.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner chooses a state tool from transition complexity rather than state size alone.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Moving every object to a reducer or mutating reducer state before returning it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show how an action names a valid transition and prevents scattered multi-setter updates.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `useState` is simplest for small, direct replacements.
`useReducer` describes changes as actions handled by one reducer.
Reducers help when transitions touch related fields or have many cases.
The reducer must be pure and return the next state.
Both Hooks still keep state local to a component tree position.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`useState` and `useReducer` both store local component state and queue renders. `useState` exposes a setter for a value. `useReducer` exposes `dispatch`; React passes the current state and dispatched action to a reducer function, and the reducer returns the next state.

I prefer `useState` when updates are direct and independent, such as a search string, an open flag, or one selected ID. The setter keeps the code close to the interaction and introduces very little structure.

I consider `useReducer` when a state object has several named transitions, when one event updates related fields together, or when the same transition logic is triggered from different places. Actions such as `{ type: 'submitted' }` or `{ type: 'failed', message }` describe what happened, and one reducer defines every legal result.

For example, a form request may move through idle, submitting, success, and error states. Several `setIsLoading`, `setError`, and `setData` calls can create impossible combinations if one path forgets a setter. A reducer can make `submit`, `resolve`, and `reject` replace the entire status model consistently.

The reducer must be pure: it calculates from state and action, does not send the request, and does not mutate the current state. Event handlers or Effects perform external work and dispatch actions when something happens. Reducer logic is easy to test with plain inputs and outputs. `useReducer` is not automatically faster, and it does not create application-wide state. It adds indirection, so a tiny boolean does not benefit. I switch when explicit transition names and centralized rules make the behaviour easier to understand than several scattered setter calls.

sections.title: useState and useReducer transition models
sections.content: The important difference is how updates are expressed. A setter says what the next value is; a dispatched action says what happened, and a reducer maps that event plus current state to a next state.

sections.title: Reducers model a small state machine
sections.content:
A reducer can encode valid phases so an error state cannot simultaneously claim success. Each action becomes one edge between states, and the default branch can reject an unknown action instead of silently producing a partial update.

Centralization also improves change review: all transitions are visible in one pure function. But actions that merely mirror setters—`setName`, `setEmail`, `setAge`—may add ceremony without clarifying a real transition model.

sections.title: Select the simpler state model
sections.content:
| Situation | useState | useReducer |
|---|---|---|
| One independent value | Best default | Usually extra ceremony |
| Several related transitions | Setters can scatter rules | Actions centralize rules |
| Update changes many fields | Possible but easy to forget one | One reducer returns a complete state |
| Testing | Test handlers/component | Test reducer as a pure function |
| Scope | Local | Local |

sections.title: Model request phases with actions
Boundary to remember
sections.content: A reducer manages state transitions, not asynchronous work. Do not fetch, write storage, or mutate the DOM inside the reducer. Dispatch before and after that work from an event handler or an appropriate Effect.
